source.title_on_document: The role of human agency in human-AI co-creativity

supplement.where: Appendix A (Experimental Platform and Paradigm, pp. 33-37) and Appendix B (Additional Results, pp. 38-42) are bound into this PDF. No separate online supplement is referenced. The OSF preregistration is linked on p. 10.
supplement.holds: Table A2 (p. 35): mixed-model coefficients and SEs for creativity, originality, usefulness. Table A3 (p. 36): mixed-model coefficients and SEs for cosine similarity to centroid. Participant-AI similarity (p. 37). Prompt-coding results (pp. 38-42).

paper_design_summary: Community college students (submitters) were randomly assigned to one of three conditions: high-agency instructions with access to a gpt-3.5 chatbot, low-agency instructions ('AI does the heavy lifting') with the same chatbot, or a human-only control told not to use AI. Each submitter wrote five alternative uses for each of three objects (brick, bubble wrap, frisbee). Online evaluators rated ideas for creativity, originality, and usefulness, and the authors measured homogeneity with embedding similarity to a leave-one-out condition-object centroid (preregistered) and HDBSCAN cluster metrics (exploratory).

studies.label: Single experiment: agency instructions and AI access on the Alternative Uses Task

assignment.what_was_assigned: Condition: high-agency instructions with AI chatbot access, low-agency instructions with AI chatbot access, or human-only control without AI
assignment.quote: After consenting, participants were randomly assigned to one of three conditions that varied whether they completed the idea-generation task with or without access to an AI chatbot
assignment.locator: p. 11, Method, Submission Phase; Figure A1, p. 33
assignment.prereg_locator: p. 10, Method, Preregistration (OSF link https://osf.io/2d7fe/overview?view_only=c34f80bd046e4c85aafdee3d2c33a74e); deviations listed p. 14, Statistical Approach

arms.name: High-Agency
arms.description: Told to use AI to expand upon their own ideas and generate even more creative ones ('Instead of asking AI to come up with ideas for you, use it to expand upon your own ideas...'); access to embedded gpt-3.5 chatbot

arms.name: Low-Agency
arms.description: Told to let AI's creative power work for them ('The beauty of AI is that it does the heavy lifting for you'); access to the same embedded gpt-3.5 chatbot

arms.name: Control (human only)
arms.description: Same AUT without a chatbot; told 'please do NOT use AI during the task'; copy-paste disabled

participants.exclusions: The paper gives a final sample of N = 150 submitters (pp. 10, 14), after three were excluded for failing an initial attention check (p. 10). It then excluded 22 noncompliant participants completely: 12 high-agency and 10 low-agency (pp. 13-14). The analyzed count of 128 is 150 minus 22; the paper does not print 128 or per-arm counts. Further trial-level exclusions: object trials in AI conditions without chat data were dropped (no AI use in 24 percent of low-agency trials and 38 percent of high-agency trials, p. 13). Ideas never drawn for evaluation were excluded from the rating analysis (p. 13). Preregistered target was N = 450 (p. 14). Not intention-to-treat.
participants.who: Community college students in the San Francisco Bay Area participating for research credits (Research Experience Program); age M = 25.1, SD = 9.2; 72 percent female. Separate evaluator sample: U.S. adults from CloudResearch Connect (N = 142).
participants.quote: Submitters were community college students in the San Francisco Bay Area (N = 150; age: M = 25.1 years, SD = 9.2; 72% female, 24% male, 1.3% non-binary, 2.7% self-described) who participated for research credits.
participants.locator: p. 10, Participants; p. 13-14, Manipulation Checks; p. 14, Statistical Approach

ai_tool.name_model: Custom chatbot web app (Vercel) built on gpt-3.5, temperature 0.7, generic helpful-assistant system prompt, embedded in Qualtrics
ai_tool.how_used: Participants in both AI arms could chat freely with the bot while generating ideas and typed their five uses per object in fields below the chat; the arms differed only in the agency instructions they read beforehand (Appendix A, p. 33; p. 12).

task.description: Alternative Uses Task: five alternative uses each for brick, bubble wrap, and frisbee (object order counterbalanced); 2,250 ideas in total
task.duration: One session, average completion time 30 minutes; no time limit (p. 12)

outcomes.name: Overall creativity rated by evaluators

outcomes.measure_detail: CloudResearch Connect adults (N = 142) rated a random stratified subset of 15 ideas each on overall creativity (Likert 1-5, rubric in Table A1). Linear mixed model with condition fixed effect and random intercepts for submitter and object (lme4). Submitters also self-rated one idea per object; those self-ratings are self-report and not listed.

outcomes.name: Homogeneity: cosine similarity of each idea to the leave-one-out condition-object centroid
outcomes.question: across_people
outcomes.measure_detail: One randomly sampled idea per participant per object; cosine similarity to the centroid of all other ideas in the same condition and object. Higher similarity means more homogeneous, so the sign is reversed relative to diversity. Directions below are coded on diversity.

contrasts.reported: Table A3, Low-Agency is reference: Intercept 0.441*** (0.015); Control -0.014 (0.019), not starred; Num.Obs. 337. Omnibus F(2, 121.67) = 3.15, p < .05, partial eta squared = .07. No Tukey test for Low-Agency vs Control printed; text says low-agency and control produced 'similarly homogeneous' ideas.
contrasts.locator: p. 36, Table A3; p. 16, Homogeneity; p. 31, Figure 2

contrasts.reported: Tukey HSD: no differences in idea homogeneity between the high-agency condition and the control condition, t(122) = 1.87, p = .15. Table A3 relative to Low-Agency: High-Agency -0.050* (0.021), Control -0.014 (0.019).
contrasts.locator: p. 16; p. 36, Table A3; p. 31, Figure 2

contrasts.reported: Table A3: High-Agency -0.050* (0.021) in cosine similarity relative to Low-Agency (Intercept 0.441). Tukey HSD: high-agency ideas less similar to the condition-object centroid than low-agency, t(125) = -2.45, p < .05. Higher diversity in the treatment arm (sign reversed from similarity).
contrasts.locator: p. 36, Table A3; p. 16; p. 31, Figure 2

diversity_detail.metric: Cosine similarity of an idea embedding to the leave-one-out centroid of the other ideas in the same condition and object (the text on p. 15 writes the formula as 1 - cosine, but Table A3 and Figure 2 report cosine similarity)
diversity_detail.computed_over: Each output against the leave-one-out centroid of its condition-object pool; one randomly sampled idea per participant per object
diversity_detail.uncertainty: Linear mixed-effects model (lme4) with condition as fixed effect and random intercepts for participants and objects; Tukey HSD pairwise comparisons; Figure 2 shows bootstrapped 95 percent CIs
diversity_detail.notes: Figure 2 condition means read roughly 0.44 (Low-Agency), 0.39 (High-Agency), 0.43 (Control); no exact arm means or SDs printed.

outcomes.name: Number of unique HDBSCAN clusters per condition-object pool (exploratory)
outcomes.question: across_people
outcomes.measure_detail: HDBSCAN on sentence embeddings, min cluster size 6, min samples 1, cluster selection epsilon 0.25, run for each object-condition combination. More clusters means more categories of uses, read as more diverse.

contrasts.reported: Permutation test (5,000 permutations) comparing maximum and minimum condition means: observed difference 3.33 clusters, driven by more clusters in control than low-agency, p = .04.

diversity_detail.embedding_model: Sentence embeddings, presumably all-MiniLM-L6-v2 (the clustering paragraph does not name the model)
diversity_detail.computed_over: All submitted ideas in each condition-object pool
diversity_detail.uncertainty: Permutation test with 5,000 permutations comparing the maximum and minimum condition means
diversity_detail.notes: Only the max-vs-min condition contrast is tested. High-Agency contrasts are shown only in Figure 3 (t-SNE plots), with no numbers.

outcomes.name: Noise ratio: share of ideas not assigned to any HDBSCAN cluster (exploratory)
outcomes.question: across_people
outcomes.measure_detail: Proportion of ideas classified as noise by HDBSCAN, read as a proxy for outlier ideas that indicate greater diversity.

contrasts.reported: Permutation test: observed difference 0.22, driven by a higher noise ratio in control than low-agency, p = .02.

diversity_detail.embedding_model: Sentence embeddings, presumably all-MiniLM-L6-v2 (not named in the clustering paragraph)
diversity_detail.computed_over: All submitted ideas in each condition-object pool
diversity_detail.uncertainty: Permutation test with 5,000 permutations comparing the maximum and minimum condition means

outcomes.name: Coefficient of variation of HDBSCAN cluster sizes (exploratory)
outcomes.question: across_people
outcomes.measure_detail: SD of cluster sizes divided by mean cluster size; higher CV means more imbalance, read as participants clustering onto one category (more homogeneous). Directions coded on diversity.

contrasts.reported: Permutation test: observed difference 0.75, driven by the low-agency condition having a significantly higher coefficient of variation than control, p = .005 (lower diversity in Low-Agency).

diversity_detail.metric: Coefficient of variation of cluster sizes
diversity_detail.embedding_model: Sentence embeddings, presumably all-MiniLM-L6-v2 (not named in the clustering paragraph)
diversity_detail.computed_over: All submitted ideas in each condition-object pool
diversity_detail.uncertainty: Permutation test with 5,000 permutations comparing the maximum and minimum condition means
diversity_detail.notes: The Discussion (p. 18) says low-agency CV was significantly greater than both the high-agency and control conditions, but the Results report only the max-vs-min test against control.

company_involvement.description: Liebscher, Rapuano, and Niederhoffer are affiliated with BetterUp Labs; authors with BetterUp affiliations are paid employees of BetterUp Inc., and A. Lee and J. Hancock are paid consultants within BetterUp Labs. BetterUp did not build the AI tool (gpt-3.5 via a custom web app).

eligibility.reason: Individuals were randomly assigned to two chatbot-access arms (different agency instructions) or a no-AI control (p. 11). The final sample is N = 150 submitters (pp. 10, 14), and after 22 noncompliers were dropped about 128 remain, well above 50. Outcomes are evaluator ratings and embedding/cluster diversity of the ideas. Caveats: the analysis is per-protocol (22 participants and AI-condition trials without chat use were excluded, and the authors write that noncompliance 'somewhat compromised the random assignment', p. 20), and the sample is far below the preregistered 450.

one_line_finding: Relative to low-agency AI use, neither high-agency AI use nor the no-AI control changed rated creativity or originality (Table A2, p. 35; ps > .60, p. 15), but high-agency ideas were less similar to their condition centroid than low-agency ideas (-0.050, SE 0.021, Table A3, p. 36; t(125) = -2.45, p < .05), and clustering showed fewer clusters, lower noise ratio, and higher cluster-size CV for low-agency than control (p. 17).
open_questions: Setting: the paper does not say whether submitters took the Qualtrics session in a supervised lab or remotely; coded online_rct, could be lab_rct.
Analyzed count: 128 is 150 minus the 22 fully excluded noncompliers and is not printed; per-arm counts are not given. Table A3 has 337 idea observations and Tukey tests show t(125) and t(122).
Whether 150 is the count at randomization: the three attention-check exclusions are called 'initial', but the paper does not say whether they came before assignment.
Usefulness inconsistency: the text reports low-agency vs control beta = 0.20, p = .04 (p. 15), but Table A2 shows Control -0.162 (0.090) with no star (p. 35).
Homogeneity metric direction: p. 15 defines the score as 1 - cosine(idea, centroid), yet Table A3, Figure 2, and p. 16 treat it as cosine similarity (higher = more homogeneous).
Figure 1 note (p. 30) describes cosine similarity points although the panels show creativity, originality, and usefulness ratings; likely a copy error.

Which AI arm serves as the primary AI-vs-no-AI record: both arms use the same open chatbot and differ only in instructions; Low-Agency ('let AI do the work') may be closer to default chatbot use, but neither arm is plain uninstructed use.
notes: Outcomes not listed because they do not bear on the three questions or are not scored on output by others: submitters' self-ratings of one own idea per object (creativity, originality, value, perceived uniqueness; p. 12, self-report, no results printed); self-reported AI helpfulness, AI as conversational partner, and intrinsic motivation (pp. 12-13); participant-AI semantic similarity between submitted ideas and the AI's suggestions, high vs low agency, ps > .05 (Appendix A, p. 37); prompt-type classification (Direct Ask: Low-Agency M = 0.84, SD = 0.29 vs High-Agency M = 0.50, SD = 0.45, t(79) = 4.01, p < .001, d = 0.91; Exploratory: High 0.46 vs Low 0.15, t(79) = 3.81, d = 0.86; pp. 41-42); chat-log behaviors (turns, duration, words per turn, copy-paste), ps > .17 (p. 38). No fluency outcome: every submitter was asked for exactly five ideas per object, although the abstract mentions ideational fluency. Rating analysis uses 1,709 evaluator ratings; ideas never sampled for evaluation were dropped (p. 13). Evaluators: CloudResearch Connect U.S. adults, N = 142, with six excluded for attention check and five for idea logging issues (p. 10); the text does not make clear whether 142 is before or after those exclusions.
